lessons.title: What “unexplained” means and the work-up behind it
lessons.objective: Define unexplained infertility as ESHRE does, complete the work-up that supports it, and recognise the tests that are not recommended.
lessons.closing: Unexplained is a diagnosis of exclusion after a complete basic work-up. More tests do not “explain” it: almost all additional tests carry a strong recommendation against.

lessons.title: Prognosis and first line: ESHRE versus NICE
lessons.objective: Decide between expectant management and active treatment by prognosis, know the evidence by outcome type, and explain why ESHRE and NICE differ.
lessons.closing: ESHRE: IUI with ovarian stimulation as first line, started according to prognosis. NICE: complete 2 years, then IUI with gonadotrophins or IVF. Neither supports stimulation alone.

lessons.title: Stimulated IUI and when to move to IVF
lessons.objective: Plan a safe stimulated IUI, individualise the move to IVF, avoid ICSI without a male factor, and not offer extras without proven benefit.
lessons.closing: Low dose and monitoring in IUI; IVF according to age, duration and previous treatment; conventional IVF without ICSI; and no scratching, antioxidants or inositol as an “extra”.

items.title: Unexplained: a diagnosis of exclusion
items.core: ESHRE defines unexplained infertility as infertility in couples with apparently normal ovarian function, fallopian tubes, uterus, cervix and pelvis, age ≤40 years (female partner) and adequate coital frequency, and with apparently normal testicular function, genito-urinary anatomy and a normal ejaculate. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It is inevitably a diagnosis of exclusion after “standard” investigations, and the proportion of couples who receive it depends on how extensive those investigations are. ESHRE notes that about 30% of infertile couples are considered unexplained and acknowledges that there is still no consensus-standardised diagnostic work-up. As in the ICMART definition of infertility, at least 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse are required before investigations start. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The guideline considers a cycle regular if it lasts 24–38 days, with bleeding of up to 8 days and a shortest-to-longest cycle variation below 7–9 days. If minimal to mild endometriosis is found incidentally at laparoscopy, ESHRE no longer considers it unexplained infertility. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE speaks of “unexplained fertility problems” and offers both partners assessment after 1 year of unprotected intercourse when there is no known or suspected cause (1.16.5). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: According to ESHRE, what age limit and minimum time trying are part of the definition of unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: “Unexplained” describes the scope of the work-up done, not a proven cause: tell the couple exactly that.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Definition by the ESHRE 2023 guideline development group; NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would do: the work-up that supports the diagnosis
items.core: For ESHRE, the work-up includes the medical, reproductive and sexual history of both partners, at least one semen analysis according to WHO criteria, a tubal patency test (HSG or HyCoSy) and an ultrasound, preferably 3D, to exclude uterine anomalies. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Semen analysis: in a laboratory with external quality control; if the first result is below the WHO lower fifth percentile reference limit (6th edition), repeat it after a 3-month interval. Tubes: HSG and HyCoSy are valid tests compared with laparoscopy and chromopertubation (strong; ⊕⊕⊕○) and comparable to each other. Uterus: ultrasound, preferably 3D (strong; ⊕○○○); MRI is not a first-line test (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Additions ESHRE does endorse: TSH and BMI as good pre-conception practice (GPP), and considering coeliac disease testing (conditional; ⊕⊕○○). With regular cycles there is no need to confirm ovulation routinely (GPP) or to measure ovarian reserve to identify the cause or predict spontaneous conception over 6–12 months (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NICE also suggests considering coeliac serology in unexplained subfertility (1.23.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which four components make up the work-up that, according to ESHRE, must be normal before calling infertility unexplained?

rows.text: ≥12 months of unprotected intercourse; woman ≤40 years
Medical, reproductive and sexual history of both
WHO semen analysis (repeat at 3 months if below the 5th percentile)
TSH and BMI (good practice); consider coeliac disease

visual.alt: Flow diagram: after at least 12 months without pregnancy and with the woman aged 40 or under, history of both partners, WHO semen analysis, HSG or HyCoSy for the tubes and ultrasound, preferably 3D, for the uterus. Note: TSH and BMI as good practice, and consider coeliac disease.

items.application: Before labelling a couple as unexplained, check that every step has been done; if one is missing, the diagnosis is provisional.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations with varying certainty (⊕○○○ to ⊕⊕⊕○), GPPs and one conditional (coeliac disease); NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would not order: uterus and pelvis with a normal ultrasound
items.core: If ultrasound assessment of the uterine cavity is normal, ESHRE recommends no further evaluation (strong; ⊕○○○), no routine diagnostic laparoscopy (strong; ⊕○○○) and no endometrial biopsy for histology without another indication (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
It also does not recommend hysteroscopy to detect and correct intrauterine abnormalities not seen at routine imaging (strong; ⊕⊕○○): the available trials are at serious risk of bias and, in first IVF cycles, there was no significant difference in live birth (RR 1.20; 95% CI 0.96–1.49; 2 RCTs, 953 women). It does not recommend the post-coital test (strong; ⊕⊕○○) and suggests not routinely measuring mid-luteal progesterone with regular cycles (conditional; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The laparoscopy recommendation was debated: HSG and HyCoSy do not detect mild endometriosis, adhesions or subtle tubal lesions, but there are insufficient data that omitting laparoscopy misses clinically relevant diagnoses in low-risk women. ESHRE advises counselling women at high tubal risk (previous PID or ectopic pregnancy) or with endometriosis about its benefits and risks. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] NICE agrees on not offering hysteroscopy unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected (1.18.16). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: With a normal uterine ultrasound in unexplained infertility, what does ESHRE say about hysteroscopy, laparoscopy and endometrial biopsy?
items.application: With a history of PID, ectopic pregnancy or endometriosis symptoms, the laparoscopy conversation changes: she is no longer the low-risk patient the recommendation addresses.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations against (very low to low certainty) and one conditional against (luteal progesterone); NICE 2026.

items.title: What I would not order: normal semen analysis and systemic tests
items.core: With a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria, ESHRE does not recommend testing sperm DNA fragmentation, anti-sperm antibodies in semen or testicular imaging (all strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
With a normal semen analysis it also does not recommend sperm chromatin condensation, sperm aneuploidy screening, HPV or microbiology testing of semen, nor serum hormone testing (strong; ⊕○○○); seminal oxidative stress is for research only. In the systemic evaluation it does not recommend serum anti-sperm antibodies, thyroid antibodies or other autoimmune testing (apart from coeliac disease), thrombophilia testing, genetic or genomic tests, vitamin D for diagnosis or prolactin (strong; ⊕○○○), nor oxidative stress in women (strong; ⊕⊕○○). With a normal TSH, no additional thyroid evaluation is recommended (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

ESHRE explains that these tests discriminate poorly between couples who would benefit from each technique, use heterogeneous and unvalidated cut-offs, and have no proven value for decision-making; it also acknowledges that the evidence is of very low quality and that the male factor is under-researched. NICE simply advises not testing sperm DNA fragmentation (1.17.6). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: With a normal semen analysis and normal TSH, name four tests ESHRE does not recommend in unexplained infertility.
items.application: Faced with a “complete” test bundle, the useful question is whether the result would change treatment; for this list, ESHRE concludes this has not been shown.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendations against, almost all with very low certainty; NICE 2026.

items.title: Immunological tests and add-ons: do not mix scales
items.core: In assisted reproduction, ESHRE does not recommend peripheral blood tests for immune parameters or uterine NK-cell testing, and rates screening hysteroscopy as “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.body:
The good practice document on add-ons uses four phrases: “recommended”; “can be considered”; “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” (not to be applied routinely at this stage; this may change with more evidence and, optionally, it can be applied to a specific patient group); and “not recommended” (because of safety concerns, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale; research settings only). Sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping sit in the third category. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]

Population and nuance: that document addresses patients in ART, and screening hysteroscopy “can be considered” in recurrent implantation failure. For couples with unexplained infertility, the specific guideline is firmer: hysteroscopy not recommended (strong; ⊕⊕○○) and fragmentation testing not recommended with a normal semen analysis (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: What is the difference between “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” and “not recommended” in the ESHRE add-ons document?
items.pearl: Always quote the source's own scale: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” is not the same as “not recommended”, and neither is a GRADE rating.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE add-ons 2023 (good practice, own 4-level scale) versus the ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility guideline (GRADE-style strength and certainty).

items.stem: She is 33 and they have been trying for 15 months. Regular cycles, normal 3D ultrasound, patent tubes on HSG and a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria. He asks for a sperm DNA fragmentation test he read about online. What is appropriate?

options.text: Explain that, with a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend it (strong recommendation) and NICE advises against doing it.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend fragmentation testing with a normal WHO semen analysis (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE advises against it (1.17.6).

options.text: Order it, because an abnormal result would indicate ICSI.
options.why: The test is not recommended and, in unexplained infertility, ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF (strong).

options.text: Order it together with anti-sperm antibodies in semen to complete the work-up.
options.why: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend anti-sperm antibodies in semen either (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Repeat the semen analysis after 3 months before deciding anything.
options.why: ESHRE advises a repeat after 3 months when the first result is below the WHO 5th percentile, not when it is normal.

items.explanation: With a normal semen analysis, additional sperm tests are not recommended in unexplained infertility: they have not been shown to change decisions or predict reproductive outcomes.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with unexplained infertility and a normal 3D ultrasound of the uterine cavity has been offered a hysteroscopy “to make the uterus perfect before IUI”. According to ESHRE, what is correct?

options.text: No further evaluation is needed; hysteroscopy for abnormalities not seen at imaging is not recommended (strong).
options.why: Correct: with a normal ultrasound no further evaluation is needed (strong; ⊕○○○) and diagnostic-operative hysteroscopy is not recommended (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: Do it, because in some series it finds lesions in more than one in ten women with a normal ultrasound.
options.why: ESHRE reports such findings (mostly polyps and septa) but no proven outcome benefit; that is why it does not recommend it.

options.text: Order a pelvic MRI to confirm a normal uterus.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend MRI as a first-line test to confirm normal uterine anatomy (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Replace it with an endometrial biopsy for histology.
options.why: Endometrial biopsy for histology is not recommended without other indications (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

items.explanation: In unexplained infertility, a normal uterine ultrasound closes the cavity assessment; hysteroscopy is reserved for clinical suspicion.

items.stem: In a woman with unexplained infertility and a normal TSH, which of these tests do ESHRE (conditional recommendation) and NICE (consider) allow for?

options.text: Coeliac serology.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE says it can be considered (conditional; ⊕⊕○○) and NICE suggests considering it (1.23.1).

options.text: Thyroid antibodies.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend thyroid antibodies or other autoimmune tests apart from coeliac disease (strong; ⊕○○○), nor further thyroid evaluation with a normal TSH.

options.text: Thrombophilia testing.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend thrombophilia testing in unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Prolactin.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend prolactin testing (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE only offers it with an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour (1.18.11).

items.explanation: Coeliac disease is the only exception ESHRE makes to its strong recommendation against autoimmune testing in unexplained infertility, and NICE agrees on considering it.

items.title: Decide by prognosis, not by label
items.core: ESHRE advises basing the decision to start active treatment on prognosis (GPP); the most important prognostic factors are age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and previous pregnancy. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Models such as Hunault's estimate the chance of spontaneous pregnancy, but none is fully evolved: Hunault's was validated only in Canadian and Dutch populations and can be used only once, at diagnosis; newer dynamic models, initially validated in Dutch and Scottish populations, are not yet in common use. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

The guideline shows why efficacy “depends”: one RCT in couples with a favourable prognosis (intermediate, per the trial title, Steures 2006) found no difference in live birth between ovarian stimulation with IUI and expectant management, while another, in poor-prognosis couples, found a striking benefit of treatment. In young women with a short duration of infertility the added benefit is small; with older age and longer duration, it increases. The couple's preferences also count. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which four prognostic factors does ESHRE highlight for deciding when to start treatment in unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: Before discussing techniques, place the couple on their four prognostic factors: age, time trying, previous pregnancies and previous treatment.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: good practice point (GPP), based on a prognosis section added after stakeholder review.

items.title: Expectant versus active: what beats waiting
items.core: ESHRE recommends IUI with ovarian stimulation as first-line treatment for unexplained infertility (strong recommendation; very low certainty, ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
Against expectant management, the guideline summarises: clomiphene with timed intercourse was not better (cumulative birth rate 13% versus 16% with 6 months of expectant management; 1 RCT, 385 couples), and natural-cycle IUI showed no significant difference in live birth (23% versus 16%). No RCTs were found of letrozole or gonadotrophins with timed intercourse versus expectant management. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Stimulated IUI versus expectant management (Cochrane review cited by ESHRE): with poor prognosis, OR for cumulative live birth 4.48 (95% CI 2.00–10.01; 1 RCT, 201 women); with moderate prognosis, OR for live birth 0.82 (0.45–1.49; 1 RCT, 253 women). Compared with natural-cycle IUI, stimulated IUI increased live birth (OR 2.07; 1.22–3.50; 4 RCTs, 396 women). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which options did not beat expectant management in the data ESHRE summarises, and in which prognosis did stimulated IUI do so?
items.pearl: Watch the outcome and the population: these are live birth and cumulative live birth data, and the benefit of stimulated IUI depends on baseline prognosis.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong recommendation with very low certainty; few, small trials per comparison.

items.title: ESHRE versus NICE: same couple, different timeline
items.core: NICE advises trying to conceive for a total of 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse before treatment (1.38.1); after that, consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophin ovarian stimulation before IVF, or offer IVF (1.38.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE's recommendations do not set that second year: they recommend stimulated IUI as first line (strong; ⊕○○○), deciding when to start on prognosis (GPP), and consider that IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Why they differ: NICE relied on a network meta-analysis and an NHS economic model that placed IVF as the most cost-effective first-line treatment; IUI with a gonadotrophin could be cost effective and is accepted as an alternative first-line option before IVF; the committee also acknowledged that some people may prefer the less invasive option. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] ESHRE argues that, in treatment-naïve patients, IVF is as effective as stimulated IUI and that the latter is considerably less invasive and costly. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: How long in total does NICE ask couples to try before treating unexplained infertility, and which two options does it offer afterwards?

rows.text: Unexplained infertility after ≥12 months and a normal work-up
ESHRE: by prognosis → stimulated IUI first line (strong, ⊕○○○)
NICE: keep trying to 2 years in total → up to 4 IUI with gonadotrophins, or IVF

visual.alt: Flow diagram: for unexplained infertility after at least 12 months and a normal work-up, ESHRE recommends deciding by prognosis and starting stimulated IUI as first line; NICE advises continuing to try until 2 years in total and then considering up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins or offering IVF. Note: neither supports ovarian stimulation alone.

items.application: Explain to the couple that the difference is one of timeline and criteria (NHS cost-effectiveness versus invasiveness and cost), not that one guideline is wrong.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: Genuine guideline discrepancy: ESHRE 2023 (European, GRADE) versus NICE 2026 (UK, with an economic model).

items.title: Myth: “a few cycles of clomiphene or letrozole to help”
items.core: NICE advises not offering ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment for unexplained fertility problems (1.38.2): its analysis found it neither effective nor cost effective. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE reaches a similar conclusion in the justification of its recommendations, not as a formal recommendation: clomiphene, letrozole, gonadotrophins or IUI on their own are not effective compared with expectant management or natural-cycle IUI. For letrozole and gonadotrophins with timed intercourse it found no RCTs against expectant management, so that part is the development group's judgement. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Between letrozole and clomiphene with timed intercourse, one RCT (172 women) found no difference in ongoing pregnancy, and another (270 women) found more clinical pregnancies with letrozole (23.07% versus 10.68%) and more multiple pregnancies with clomiphene. The guideline reports no live birth data for this comparison and makes no recommendation on which drug to use. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: What does NICE say about ovarian stimulation without IUI in unexplained infertility?
items.pearl: More clinical pregnancies in a small RCT do not equal more live births: that outcome is not reported for this comparison.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: NICE 2026 (explicit recommendation against); ESHRE 2023 (conclusion in the justification, not a formal recommendation).

items.title: Oil-based HSG: more than a test
items.core: ESHRE considers HSG (tubal flushing) with oil-soluble contrast preferable to water-soluble contrast and asks that its risks and benefits be discussed with all couples with unexplained infertility (conditional; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited, oil-based contrast probably increases clinical pregnancy compared with water-based contrast (OR 1.42; 95% CI 1.10–1.85; 6 RCTs, 2598 women); live birth was reported in 3 RCTs, two favouring oil and one showing no difference. In the 5-year follow-up of the largest trial (1119 women) there were more live births with oil-based contrast (RR 1.11; 1.03–1.20) and a shorter time to ongoing pregnancy. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

Risks: intravasation is more frequent with oil-based contrast (OR 5.00; 2.25–11.12), with no difference in infection or haemorrhage; four cases of serious embolism have been reported since 1928, so ESHRE stresses performing HSG under fluoroscopic control (the guideline says “fluorescence guidance”) so that it can be stopped in time. Part of the evidence comes from ovulatory women with diagnoses other than unexplained infertility, although, according to ESHRE, the largest trial (1119 women) included women with unexplained infertility. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.recall: Which HSG contrast does ESHRE prefer in unexplained infertility, with what strength, and what is its main risk?
items.pearl: If HSG is already indicated, the type of contrast deserves a conversation with the couple, not just a technical choice.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: conditional recommendation (⊕⊕○○); requires shared decision-making.

items.stem: How does ESHRE 2023 grade its recommendation of IUI with ovarian stimulation as first line in unexplained infertility?

options.text: Strong, with very low certainty of evidence (⊕○○○).
options.why: Correct: it is a strong recommendation supported by very low certainty evidence; strength and certainty are different things.

options.text: Strong, with high certainty (⊕⊕⊕⊕).
options.why: None of this guideline's recommendations is supported by high-quality evidence.

options.text: Conditional, with low certainty (⊕⊕○○).
options.why: The recommendation is strong; the conditional one with ⊕○○○ is that IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI.

options.text: A good practice point, with no evidence graded.
options.why: It is an evidence-based recommendation; the related good practice point is deciding when to start based on prognosis.

items.explanation: ESHRE separates strength of recommendation from certainty of evidence: a recommendation can be strong even when certainty is very low, and that is worth explaining to the couple.

items.stem: Couple seen in the NHS (UK); she is 31. After 12 months without pregnancy, the full work-up is normal. According to NICE NG257, what is appropriate now?

options.text: Advise them to keep trying until 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse in total before treatment.
options.why: Correct: NICE advises a total of 2 years before treatment (1.38.1).

options.text: Clomiphene with timed intercourse for 6 cycles.
options.why: NICE advises against ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment (1.38.2).

options.text: Immediate IVF.
options.why: For unexplained infertility, NICE offers IVF after 2 years without conceiving, with or without IUI (1.39.3).

options.text: IUI with gonadotrophin stimulation starting now.
options.why: NICE positions stimulated IUI for those who have already tried for 2 years (1.38.3); this would be closer to ESHRE, which decides timing by prognosis.

items.explanation: NICE structures treatment of unexplained infertility over time: 2 years in total, then up to 4 IUI cycles with gonadotrophins, or IVF.

items.stem: In the 385-couple RCT in unexplained infertility summarised by ESHRE, what did clomiphene with timed intercourse show compared with 6 months of expectant management?

options.text: It did not improve the outcome: cumulative birth rate 13% versus 16% with expectant management.
options.why: Correct: that is ESHRE's summary, which also found no cost benefit of clomiphene over expectant management.

options.text: It doubled the live birth rate.
options.why: There was no benefit; the numerically higher figure was in the expectant group.

options.text: It increased clinical pregnancy, but the trial did not measure live birth.
options.why: The trial reported cumulative births and time to a pregnancy leading to live birth, with no advantage for clomiphene.

options.text: It improved cumulative live birth only in poor-prognosis couples.
options.why: That poor-prognosis benefit belongs to IUI with ovarian stimulation, not to clomiphene with timed intercourse.

items.explanation: Oral stimulation with timed intercourse does not beat waiting in unexplained infertility; what ESHRE recommends is IUI combined with stimulation.

items.title: What I would do: stimulated IUI with a low dose and monitoring
items.core: To avoid multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), ESHRE advises using gonadotrophins for IUI only in a low-dose regimen with adequate monitoring (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In its justification, ESHRE regards IUI in a stimulated cycle for three to six cycles as first line, with low-dose gonadotrophins to avoid a high number of growing follicles; according to the latest European studies, a low dose greatly reduces multiple pregnancy without significantly reducing live birth. Compared with expectant management, the OR for multiple pregnancy with stimulated IUI was 3.01 (95% CI 0.47–19.28; 2 RCTs), a very wide interval. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE positions up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophins before IVF (1.38.3) and asks that ovulation induction or ovarian stimulation agents be limited to the lowest effective dose and duration (1.54.3). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: What measure does ESHRE propose to reduce multiple pregnancy and OHSS in stimulated IUI, and how many cycles do ESHRE and NICE envisage?
items.application: When planning IUI, agree in advance with the couple how many cycles you will do and what will happen if the response is multifollicular.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: GPP; 3–6 cycles in ESHRE's justification versus “up to 4” in the NICE 2026 recommendation.

items.title: When to move to IVF?
items.core: ESHRE considers that IVF is probably not recommended over IUI with ovarian stimulation (conditional; ⊕○○○) and expects the decision to be individualised by age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and previous pregnancy (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited (8 RCTs), live birth was higher with IVF than with stimulated IUI (RR 1.54; 95% CI 1.04–2.28; 7 RCTs, 1391 women), with no significant difference in multiple pregnancy or OHSS. In treatment-naïve women under 38 there was no difference (RR 1.01; 0.88–1.15; 3 RCTs, 925 women); from 38 onwards it favoured IVF (RR 2.15; 1.16–4.00; a single RCT, 154 women). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE offers IVF before the 42nd birthday to people with unexplained fertility problems who have not conceived after 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse, with or without IUI (1.39.3): 3 full cycles under 40, with up to 3 more considered (1.39.6, 1.39.7), and 1 full cycle at 40–41 if they have not had IVF before (1.39.9). A full cycle comprises one episode of ovarian stimulation and the transfer of all resulting fresh and frozen embryos (1.39.4). That 42nd-birthday limit is an access criterion for NHS-funded IVF, not a definition: it does not contradict the ≤40-year limit in ESHRE's definition. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which subgroup showed no live birth difference between IVF and stimulated IUI in the data ESHRE summarises?
items.pearl: The 38-and-over finding rests on a single RCT: it is an argument for individualising earlier, not a validated cut-off.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: conditional (⊕○○○) + GPP; NICE 2026: NHS access criteria based on an economic analysis.

items.title: What I would not do: “just in case” ICSI without a male factor
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in couples with unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the RCTs reviewed, live birth was similar: 35.5% with IVF versus 36.7% with ICSI in a subgroup of 382 couples (RR 1.03; 95% CI 0.79–1.35), and 46.7% versus 50% in an RCT of 60 couples. ESHRE adds the evidence of no difference in non-male factor infertility and the greater resources and costs of ICSI. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

NICE advises not using ICSI for non-male factor fertility problems if semen parameters are normal (1.50.3) and considering it with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2). The ESHRE add-ons document also rates ICSI for non-male factor infertility as “not recommended”. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]]
items.recall: When does NICE consider ICSI, and why is it not recommended in unexplained infertility?
items.application: If the couple asks for ICSI “to be sure”, separate two questions: whether there is an indication (abnormal semen, previous failed fertilisation) and whether it improves live birth without one (it does not).

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: strong against (⊕○○○); NICE 2026; ESHRE add-ons 2023 (not recommended).

items.title: What I would not offer as an “extra help”
items.core: ESHRE states that endometrial scratching should not be offered for unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕⊕○○). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]
items.body:
In the most recent RCT with timed intercourse (220 women), live birth was 9% versus 7% with a sham procedure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.50–4.03); overall, ESHRE concludes that the evidence does not show better pregnancy outcomes when scratching is performed before intercourse or IUI, although a few small individual RCTs did report more pregnancies. ESHRE also considers adjunct oral antioxidants in women and men (conditional; ⊕○○○), acupuncture in women (conditional; ⊕⊕○○) and inositol in women (conditional; ⊕○○○) probably not recommended. [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]]

What it does endorse as good practice: psychological support, including psychotherapy, when needed, and a healthy diet with regular exercise, supported by behavioural therapy when necessary (GPP). NICE also does not offer scratching or hysteroscopy as pre-treatment to improve IVF outcomes (1.40.1, 1.40.2). [[ref:eshre-2023-unexplained-infertility]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: How strongly does ESHRE advise against endometrial scratching, and how strongly against antioxidants and inositol, in unexplained infertility?
items.application: From an integrative perspective, the space ESHRE does support in this indication is lifestyle and psychological support, not antioxidants or inositol.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2023: scratching, strong against (⊕⊕○○); antioxidants, acupuncture and inositol, conditional against; lifestyle and psychological support, GPP. NICE 2026.

items.stem: A 39-year-old woman; 3 years of unexplained infertility, no previous treatment. Which statement about IVF versus stimulated IUI is most faithful to ESHRE 2023?

options.text: IVF is probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional), but the decision is individualised by age, duration and history; from 38 onwards, a single RCT favoured IVF.
options.why: Correct: it combines the conditional recommendation, the GPP on individualising and the subgroup finding with its limitation.

options.text: ESHRE recommends first-line IVF from age 38 (strong recommendation).
options.why: ESHRE makes no age-based recommendation; the 38-year finding comes from a single RCT within a sensitivity analysis.

options.text: IVF does not increase live birth over stimulated IUI in any analysis.
options.why: In the overall analysis live birth was higher with IVF (RR 1.54); equivalence was seen in treatment-naïve women under 38.

options.text: Because of her age, IVF with ICSI is recommended.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in unexplained infertility (strong), and age is not an ICSI indication in these guidelines.

items.explanation: The general recommendation favours starting with stimulated IUI, but ESHRE asks for individualisation: age, duration and history can justify IVF, with subgroup evidence that is still limited.

items.stem: A couple with unexplained infertility is about to start IVF; the semen analysis is normal. They ask for ICSI “to make sure of fertilisation”. What is appropriate?

options.text: Conventional IVF, explaining that ICSI is not recommended in this situation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE does not recommend ICSI over conventional IVF in unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○) and NICE advises against it with normal semen (1.50.3).

options.text: ICSI, because it increases live birth in unexplained infertility.
options.why: The RCTs reviewed by ESHRE show similar live birth (for example, 35.5% versus 36.7%).

options.text: ICSI, adding IMSI to select the sperm better.
options.why: Besides ICSI not being indicated, NICE advises against IMSI as an adjunct to ICSI (1.50.4).

options.text: Decide based on a sperm DNA fragmentation test.
options.why: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend that test (strong) and NICE advises against it (1.17.6).

items.explanation: Without a male factor or previous failed fertilisation, ICSI adds cost and resources without improving live birth in unexplained infertility.

items.stem: Before her first stimulated IUI, a patient with unexplained infertility asks about the “endometrial scratch” recommended on a forum. What is correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: It should not be offered (strong recommendation): overall, the evidence with timed intercourse and with IUI does not show better pregnancy outcomes.
options.why: Correct: “should not be offered for unexplained infertility” (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: It is recommended in the luteal phase of the cycle before IUI.
options.why: Timing varied between trials, but none justified recommending it; the recommendation is against.

options.text: It is probably not recommended (conditional), but it is a reasonable option if the patient wishes.
options.why: The strength is strong, not conditional; the conditional recommendations against are antioxidants, acupuncture and inositol.

options.text: It is only useful with timed intercourse, not before IUI.
options.why: In the most recent RCT with timed intercourse, live birth was 9% versus 7%, with no significant difference.

items.explanation: Scratching is a cheap outpatient procedure, but in unexplained infertility the evidence shows no benefit and ESHRE strongly advises against it.

items.stem: What does ESHRE propose to limit multiple pregnancy and OHSS in stimulated IUI for unexplained infertility?

options.text: Use gonadotrophins only in a low-dose regimen, with adequate monitoring.
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE's good practice point accompanying the stimulated IUI recommendation.

options.text: Replace gonadotrophins with clomiphene.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend a specific drug, and in one cited RCT with timed intercourse (not IUI) multiple pregnancy was higher with clomiphene than with letrozole.

options.text: Use natural-cycle IUI as first line.
options.why: Natural-cycle IUI did not beat expectant management, and stimulated IUI increased live birth compared with it (OR 2.07).

options.text: Avoid IUI and move straight to IVF in all couples.
options.why: ESHRE considers IVF probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional) and asks for individualisation.

items.explanation: The safety of stimulated IUI depends mainly on dose and monitoring: fewer growing follicles, less risk of multiple pregnancy.

items.stem: Under the ESHRE 2023 definition, which female age limit and which minimum time of regular unprotected intercourse are part of the diagnosis of unexplained infertility?

options.text: ≤35 years and at least 6 months.
options.why: Neither the age nor the duration matches ESHRE's definition (≤40 years; at least 12 months).

options.text: ≤42 years and at least 24 months.
options.why: This mixes up NICE criteria: the 42nd birthday is an NHS IVF access criterion and 2 years is NICE's timeframe before treatment, not ESHRE's definition.

options.text: No age limit and at least 12 months.
options.why: ESHRE's definition does include a female age limit: ≤40 years.

options.text: ≤40 years and at least 12 months.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE's definition includes female age ≤40 years and, as in ICMART, at least 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.

items.explanation: ESHRE: apparently normal ovarian function, tubes, uterus, cervix and pelvis, woman ≤40 years, adequate coital frequency and an apparently normal male factor, after at least 12 months of regular unprotected intercourse.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman labelled as having unexplained infertility after a complete basic work-up undergoes laparoscopy for another reason, and minimal endometriosis is found incidentally. According to ESHRE, what happens to her diagnosis?

options.text: It is no longer considered unexplained infertility.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE states that if minimal to mild endometriosis is found incidentally at laparoscopy, it is no longer considered unexplained infertility.

options.text: It remains unexplained, because minimal endometriosis does not count.
options.why: ESHRE is explicit: minimal to mild endometriosis found at laparoscopy takes the couple out of the unexplained category.

options.text: It remains unexplained until endometriosis is confirmed by endometrial biopsy.
options.why: Endometrial biopsy is not part of this criterion; ESHRE does not recommend it for histology without another indication.

options.text: It only stops being unexplained if the endometriosis is stage III–IV.
options.why: ESHRE refers precisely to minimal to mild endometriosis, not only to advanced stages.

items.explanation: “Unexplained” depends on how extensive the work-up is: a laparoscopic finding such as minimal to mild endometriosis changes the label according to ESHRE.

items.stem: Which of these cycle patterns meets the regular-cycle criterion used in the ESHRE 2023 unexplained infertility guideline?

options.text: Cycles of 22 to 26 days, with 5 days of bleeding.
options.why: A 22-day cycle falls below the 24-day minimum.

options.text: Cycles of 25 to 40 days, with 4 days of bleeding.
options.why: 40 days exceeds the 38-day maximum, and a 15-day variation exceeds 7–9 days.

options.text: Cycles of 26 to 31 days, with 5 days of bleeding.
options.why: Correct: it lies within 24–38 days, with bleeding ≤8 days and a shortest-to-longest variation below 7–9 days.

options.text: Cycles of 28 to 30 days, with 10 days of bleeding.
options.why: Ten days of bleeding exceeds the 8-day maximum.

items.explanation: ESHRE considers a cycle regular if it lasts 24–38 days, with bleeding of up to 8 days and a shortest-to-longest cycle variation below 7–9 days.

items.stem: She is 32 and they have been trying for 14 months, with regular cycles. You already have both partners' history, a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria and a normal 3D ultrasound. According to ESHRE, what is missing before calling it unexplained infertility?

options.text: A diagnostic laparoscopy with chromopertubation.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend routine diagnostic laparoscopy (strong; ⊕○○○); HSG or HyCoSy are the proposed tubal tests.

options.text: An AMH test to identify the cause.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend measuring ovarian reserve to identify the cause or to predict spontaneous conception (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: A tubal patency test: HSG or HyCoSy.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE's work-up includes a tubal patency test, and HSG and HyCoSy are valid tests (strong; ⊕⊕⊕○).

options.text: A mid-luteal progesterone to confirm ovulation.
options.why: With regular cycles there is no need to confirm ovulation routinely (GPP), and ESHRE suggests not routinely measuring luteal progesterone (conditional; ⊕○○○).

items.explanation: Work-up per ESHRE: history of both partners, at least one WHO semen analysis, a tubal patency test (HSG or HyCoSy) and an ultrasound, preferably 3D. “Unexplained” is a diagnosis of exclusion: without the tubal test, the work-up is not complete.

items.stem: In a couple's work-up, the first semen analysis, done in a laboratory with external quality control, falls below the WHO lower fifth percentile reference limit (6th edition). What does ESHRE advise?

options.text: Repeat it after a 3-month interval.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE advises repeating the semen analysis after 3 months if the first is below the WHO 5th percentile.

options.text: Label the infertility as unexplained and start IUI.
options.why: The definition of unexplained requires an apparently normal ejaculate; a low result should be repeated first.

options.text: Repeat it after one week to confirm it as soon as possible.
options.why: The interval ESHRE advises is 3 months, not one week.

options.text: Order sperm DNA fragmentation testing directly instead of repeating it.
options.why: The step ESHRE advises after a low first semen analysis is to repeat it after 3 months.

items.explanation: ESHRE asks for at least one WHO semen analysis in a laboratory with external quality control, repeated after 3 months if the first falls below the 5th percentile.

items.stem: In the work-up of unexplained infertility, what does ESHRE advise about uterine imaging?

options.text: Pelvic MRI first line, because of its higher resolution.
options.why: ESHRE states that MRI is not a first-line test (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy for all women.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend hysteroscopy to look for abnormalities not seen at routine imaging (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: 2D ultrasound; ESHRE advises against 3D as unnecessary.
options.why: It is the other way round: ESHRE recommends ultrasound, preferably 3D.

options.text: Ultrasound, preferably 3D (strong); MRI is not a first-line test (strong).
options.why: Correct: both are strong recommendations with very low certainty (⊕○○○).

items.explanation: To exclude uterine anomalies, ESHRE proposes ultrasound, preferably 3D; MRI is not first line.

items.stem: A 33-year-old woman with unexplained infertility after a normal basic work-up; she has had pelvic inflammatory disease and a previous ectopic pregnancy. She asks whether she should have a laparoscopy. What is most faithful to ESHRE?

options.text: Tell her that ESHRE does not recommend laparoscopy in any woman with unexplained infertility.
options.why: This overgeneralises: the recommendation is against routine laparoscopy, and ESHRE reserves it for higher-risk women.

options.text: Consider laparoscopy, because ESHRE reserves it for women with an abnormal HSG or at risk of tubo-peritoneal disease (PID, previous ectopic pregnancy, known or suspected endometriosis).
options.why: Correct: the strong recommendation against routine laparoscopy addresses women at low risk for tubal pathology; ESHRE states it should be reserved for women with an abnormal HSG or at risk of tubo-peritoneal disease because of PID, a previous ectopic pregnancy, or known or suspected endometriosis.

options.text: Tell her that laparoscopy is mandatory before any treatment.
options.why: ESHRE reserves it for women with an abnormal HSG or at risk of tubo-peritoneal disease; it does not make it mandatory for everyone.

options.text: Explain that HSG already rules out mild endometriosis and adhesions, so it adds nothing.
options.why: ESHRE acknowledges that HSG and HyCoSy do not detect mild endometriosis, adhesions or subtle tubal lesions.

items.explanation: The recommendation against routine laparoscopy (strong; ⊕○○○) rests on limited clinical benefit and on the fact that it is not risk-free; ESHRE states it should be reserved for women with an abnormal HSG or at risk of tubo-peritoneal disease (PID, previous ectopic pregnancy, known or suspected endometriosis).

items.stem: In unexplained infertility with regular cycles, what is ESHRE's position on the post-coital test and on mid-luteal progesterone?

options.text: Post-coital test not recommended (strong); it suggests not routinely measuring luteal progesterone (conditional).
options.why: Correct: post-coital test, strong against (⊕⊕○○); routine mid-luteal progesterone, conditional against (⊕○○○).

options.text: Luteal progesterone not recommended (strong); post-coital test conditionally discouraged.
options.why: It is the other way round: the strong one concerns the post-coital test and the conditional one, progesterone.

options.text: Both recommended to complete the cervical and ovulatory work-up.
options.why: ESHRE recommends neither routinely in this population.

options.text: Both are only good practice points (GPP), with no direction.
options.why: They are recommendations with a direction against: one strong and one conditional.

items.explanation: Distinguish the strength: the post-coital test carries a strong recommendation against; mid-luteal progesterone with regular cycles, a conditional one against.

items.stem: ESHRE summarises that, in first IVF cycles, routine hysteroscopy versus none gave a live birth RR of 1.20 (95% CI 0.96–1.49; 2 RCTs, 953 women). How should this be read?

options.text: Hysteroscopy has been shown to increase live birth by 20%.
options.why: The point estimate is 1.20, but the interval includes 1: it is not a significant difference.

options.text: There was no significant difference: the interval includes 1.
options.why: Correct: a 95% CI crossing 1 does not show benefit; ESHRE also notes serious risk of bias in those trials.

options.text: Hysteroscopy reduces live birth.
options.why: An RR above 1 with an interval that crosses 1 does not indicate a reduction.

options.text: It shows with high certainty that hysteroscopy has no effect at all.
options.why: Non-significant does not mean a proven null effect, and certainty is low (⊕⊕○○) because of risk of bias.

items.explanation: This is why ESHRE does not recommend hysteroscopy to detect and correct abnormalities not seen at routine imaging (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with unexplained infertility and a normal TSH. She brings a list: thyroid antibodies, thrombophilia testing, vitamin D and prolactin. According to ESHRE, which of them are recommended?

options.text: Only thyroid antibodies, because a normal TSH is not enough.
options.why: With a normal TSH, ESHRE recommends no further thyroid evaluation, including antibodies (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Only thrombophilia, in case heparin needs to be added.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend thrombophilia testing in unexplained infertility (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: Only prolactin and vitamin D, because they are cheap.
options.why: Both are on the list of tests ESHRE does not recommend (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: None: ESHRE does not recommend any of those tests (strong; ⊕○○○).
options.why: Correct: with a normal TSH it recommends no further thyroid evaluation, nor thrombophilia testing, vitamin D for diagnosis or prolactin.

items.explanation: In the systemic evaluation, ESHRE keeps only TSH and BMI (good practice) and considering coeliac disease; the rest of the list carries a strong recommendation against.

items.stem: In a couple with unexplained infertility and a normal semen analysis by WHO criteria, the male partner is offered testicular ultrasound, serum hormones and a seminal oxidative stress test. What does ESHRE say?

options.text: It recommends testicular ultrasound to rule out a varicocele.
options.why: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE does not recommend testicular imaging (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: It recommends serum hormones, because semen analysis does not assess testicular function.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend serum hormone testing with a normal semen analysis (strong; ⊕○○○).

options.text: It does not recommend testicular imaging or serum hormones (strong), and seminal oxidative stress is for research only.
options.why: Correct: with a normal semen analysis, both carry a strong recommendation against (⊕○○○) and seminal oxidative stress is reserved for research.

options.text: It recommends seminal oxidative stress testing to decide on antioxidants.
options.why: Seminal oxidative stress is for research only, and adjunct oral antioxidants are probably not recommended (conditional).

items.explanation: With a normal semen analysis, ESHRE recommends no further male testing: neither testicular imaging nor serum hormones, and seminal oxidative stress only in research.

items.stem: What reasoning does ESHRE give for not recommending additional tests (sperm, autoimmune, thrombophilia, genetic) in unexplained infertility?

options.text: High-quality RCTs showed that doing them reduces live birth.
options.why: The evidence is of very low quality; the argument is lack of proven usefulness, not harm shown in RCTs.

options.text: It has been shown with high certainty that none of them has any value.
options.why: Almost all of these recommendations have very low certainty (⊕○○○); ESHRE also acknowledges that the male factor is under-researched.

options.text: Only because of their cost, even though they change treatment.
options.why: ESHRE points out precisely that they have not been shown to change decisions.

options.text: They discriminate poorly between couples who would benefit from each technique, use heterogeneous and unvalidated cut-offs, and have no proven value for decision-making.
options.why: Correct: this is ESHRE's justification, which also acknowledges that the evidence is of very low quality.

items.explanation: ESHRE justifies these recommendations by the lack of proven usefulness of the tests for decision-making, while acknowledging that the evidence is of very low quality (⊕○○○).

items.stem: In ESHRE's good practice document on add-ons in assisted reproduction, what does the category “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” mean?

options.text: Research settings only, because of safety concerns, lack of efficacy or lack of biological rationale.
options.why: That is the definition of “not recommended”, the fourth category.

options.text: It is equivalent to a strong GRADE recommendation against.
options.why: It is the document's own scale; none of its categories is a GRADE rating.

options.text: Do not apply it routinely at this stage; this may change with more evidence and, optionally, it can be applied to a specific patient group.
options.why: Correct: this is how the document defines this third category of its four-level scale.

options.text: It is equivalent to “can be considered”.
options.why: “Can be considered” is a separate, more favourable category.

items.explanation: The add-ons scale has four phrases: “recommended”, “can be considered”, “currently not recommended for routine clinical use” and “not recommended”. Always quote the source's own one.

items.stem: In which category does the ESHRE add-ons document place sperm DNA damage testing, endometrial scratching and KIR/HLA genotyping?

options.text: “Not recommended”.
options.why: In the add-ons document, these three sit in “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”, not in “not recommended”.

options.text: “Currently not recommended for routine clinical use”.
options.why: Correct: all three sit in the third category of the scale.

options.text: “Can be considered”.
options.why: None of the three is in that category.

options.text: “Recommended” in selected patients.
options.why: None of the three is recommended in the document.

items.explanation: Do not mix scales: the specific unexplained infertility guideline is firmer, with a strong recommendation against scratching and against fragmentation testing with a normal semen analysis.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with unexplained infertility, no previous treatment and a normal uterine ultrasound. A colleague proposes hysteroscopy, quoting ESHRE as saying it “can be considered”. What is correct?

options.text: That add-ons “can be considered” refers to recurrent implantation failure; in unexplained infertility, ESHRE does not recommend hysteroscopy (strong).
options.why: Correct: each recommendation's population must be respected; the specific guideline is strong against (⊕⊕○○).

options.text: The colleague is right: “can be considered” applies to any ART patient.
options.why: For screening hysteroscopy in general, the document uses “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”; “can be considered” is for recurrent implantation failure.

options.text: Do it, because NICE offers it routinely before IUI.
options.why: NICE does not offer hysteroscopy unless a uterine or endometrial abnormality is clinically suspected.

options.text: Do it only if AMH is low.
options.why: Neither source links hysteroscopy to AMH.

items.explanation: Same test, different population and scale: add-ons (ART; “can be considered” only in recurrent implantation failure) versus the unexplained infertility guideline (strong against).

items.stem: ESHRE highlights four prognostic factors for deciding when to start treatment in unexplained infertility. Which of these is NOT one of them?

options.text: Age.
options.why: Age is one of the four most important prognostic factors according to ESHRE.

options.text: AMH.
options.why: Correct: it is not among the four factors, and ESHRE does not recommend measuring ovarian reserve to predict spontaneous conception in this population.

options.text: Duration of infertility.
options.why: Duration is one of the four prognostic factors.

options.text: Previous pregnancy.
options.why: Previous pregnancy is one of the four factors (together with previous treatment).

items.explanation: ESHRE's four factors: age, duration of infertility, previous treatment and previous pregnancy. The decision to treat is based on prognosis (GPP).

items.stem: What limitation does ESHRE point out about the Hunault model for estimating spontaneous pregnancy?

options.text: It is a dynamic model that must be recalculated at every visit.
options.why: It is the other way round: Hunault's model is used only at diagnosis; dynamic models are newer and not yet in common use.

options.text: It predicts live birth with IVF, not spontaneous pregnancy.
options.why: ESHRE cites it as a model of the chance of spontaneous pregnancy.

options.text: ESHRE requires it before any treatment.
options.why: ESHRE advises deciding on prognosis (GPP), but does not require a specific model, and acknowledges their limitations.

options.text: It was validated only in Canadian and Dutch populations and can be used only once, at diagnosis.
options.why: Correct: that is how ESHRE describes it, considering that no model is fully evolved.

items.explanation: Prognostic models help, but none is fully evolved: Hunault's has limited geographic validation and single use at diagnosis.

items.stem: Two couples with unexplained infertility and a normal work-up: A) she is 29, 13 months trying; B) she is 39, 4 years trying. Neither has previous pregnancies or treatment. Following ESHRE's reasoning, what is most likely?

options.text: The added benefit of active treatment is greater in couple B.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE explains that with older age and longer duration the added benefit increases, and that in young women with a short duration it is small.

options.text: The added benefit is greater in couple A, because she is younger.
options.why: In young women with a short duration of infertility, ESHRE describes a small added benefit.

options.text: The benefit is the same, because both carry the same unexplained label.
options.why: ESHRE advises deciding by prognosis, not by the label.

options.text: Neither should be treated before 5 years of trying.
options.why: Neither guideline proposes that timeframe; ESHRE decides by prognosis and NICE speaks of 2 years.

items.explanation: The efficacy of active treatment “depends” on baseline prognosis; the couple's preferences also count.

items.stem: In the data ESHRE summarises for unexplained infertility, which comparison showed a statistically significant increase in live birth?

options.text: Natural-cycle IUI versus expectant management: 23% versus 16%.
options.why: ESHRE summarises that this difference was not significant.

options.text: Stimulated IUI versus expectant management with moderate prognosis: OR 0.82 (0.45–1.49).
options.why: The interval includes 1: no significant difference.

options.text: Stimulated IUI versus natural-cycle IUI: OR 2.07 (95% CI 1.22–3.50).
options.why: Correct: the interval does not include 1 (4 RCTs, 396 women).

options.text: Clomiphene with timed intercourse versus expectant management: 13% versus 16%.
options.why: Clomiphene with timed intercourse was not better than expectant management.

items.explanation: Read the confidence interval: of the comparisons offered, only stimulated versus natural-cycle IUI shows an increase in live birth whose interval excludes 1; versus expectant management, the benefit appears only with poor prognosis and for cumulative live birth.

items.stem: In poor-prognosis couples, the Cochrane review cited by ESHRE gives an OR for cumulative live birth of 4.48 (95% CI 2.00–10.01; 1 RCT, 201 women) for stimulated IUI versus expectant management. What is the most accurate reading?

options.text: It is not significant, because the interval is very wide.
options.why: A wide interval indicates imprecision, but 2.00–10.01 does not include 1: it is significant.

options.text: It shows the same benefit in couples with moderate prognosis.
options.why: With moderate prognosis, the OR was 0.82 (0.45–1.49), with no difference.

options.text: A significant benefit, but from a single RCT and with a wide interval.
options.why: Correct: the interval excludes 1, but it comes from a single RCT of 201 women and is very wide; ESHRE rates the certainty behind its stimulated IUI recommendation as very low (⊕○○○).

options.text: It is high-certainty evidence for stimulated IUI.
options.why: ESHRE rates the certainty of its stimulated IUI recommendation as very low (⊕○○○).

items.explanation: The benefit of stimulated IUI depends on baseline prognosis: striking with poor prognosis, not shown with moderate prognosis.

items.stem: What evidence did ESHRE find on letrozole or gonadotrophins with timed intercourse versus expectant management in unexplained infertility?

options.text: It found no RCTs for those comparisons.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE states that no RCTs were found; its conclusion about them is the development group's judgement.

options.text: Several RCTs showed more live births with letrozole.
options.why: No RCTs of letrozole with timed intercourse versus expectant management were found.

options.text: A 385-couple RCT with gonadotrophins that showed no benefit.
options.why: The 385-couple RCT assessed clomiphene with timed intercourse, not gonadotrophins.

options.text: A meta-analysis showing more multiple pregnancies without more live births.
options.why: For these comparisons against expectant management there were no RCTs to meta-analyse.

items.explanation: Absence of RCTs is not evidence of inefficacy: for letrozole and gonadotrophins with timed intercourse, ESHRE's conclusion is the development group's judgement.

items.stem: Which statement correctly summarises the difference between ESHRE 2023 and NICE NG257 on first-line treatment of unexplained infertility?

options.text: Both require 2 years of trying before any treatment.
options.why: ESHRE's recommendations do not set that second year: they decide by prognosis.

options.text: ESHRE recommends IVF first line and NICE recommends IUI.
options.why: It is essentially inverted: ESHRE considers IVF probably not recommended over stimulated IUI, and NICE offers IVF as an option after the 2 years.

options.text: Both recommend starting with clomiphene and timed intercourse.
options.why: Neither supports ovarian stimulation alone; NICE explicitly advises against it (1.38.2).

options.text: ESHRE recommends stimulated IUI as first line, deciding when to start on prognosis; NICE advises trying for 2 years in total and then considering up to 4 IUI cycles with gonadotrophins or offering IVF.
options.why: Correct: this is the genuine discrepancy between the two guidelines (ESHRE: strong, ⊕○○○, + GPP; NICE 1.38.1 and 1.38.3).

items.explanation: The difference is one of timeline and criteria, not that one guideline is wrong.

items.stem: Why do NICE and ESHRE reach different positions on IVF versus stimulated IUI in unexplained infertility?

options.text: NICE found that IUI increases the risk of severe OHSS.
options.why: That is not NICE's argument; its reasoning is about cost-effectiveness.

options.text: NICE relied on a network meta-analysis and an NHS economic model that placed IVF as the most cost-effective first-line treatment; ESHRE argues that, in treatment-naïve patients, IVF is as effective as stimulated IUI, which is less invasive and costly.
options.why: Correct: this is the explanation the guidelines themselves give; NICE also accepts IUI with a gonadotrophin as an alternative first-line option.

options.text: ESHRE relied on an economic model and NICE only on RCTs.
options.why: It is the other way round: the economic model is NICE's, for the NHS.

options.text: They use different definitions of unexplained infertility.
options.why: The discrepancy is explained by cost-effectiveness versus invasiveness and cost, not by the definition.

items.explanation: NICE: NHS cost-effectiveness (accepting IUI with a gonadotrophin as an alternative); ESHRE: similar efficacy in treatment-naïve patients and the lower invasiveness and cost of IUI.

items.stem: What is the guidelines' position on ovarian stimulation alone (without IUI) in unexplained infertility?

options.text: NICE advises not offering it (1.38.2); ESHRE reaches a similar conclusion in its justification, not as a formal recommendation.
options.why: Correct: NICE found it neither effective nor cost effective; in ESHRE it is a conclusion in the justification.

options.text: ESHRE has a formal strong recommendation against letrozole with timed intercourse.
options.why: This overstates ESHRE's position: it is a conclusion in the justification, and for letrozole it found no RCTs against expectant management.

options.text: NICE recommends up to 6 cycles of letrozole before IUI.
options.why: NICE advises not offering ovarian stimulation as a stand-alone treatment.

options.text: Both recommend it as first line in young women.
options.why: Neither supports ovarian stimulation alone.

items.explanation: Do not overstate the strength: NICE has an explicit recommendation against; ESHRE, a conclusion in the justification of its recommendations.

items.stem: A colleague says: “In unexplained infertility, letrozole with timed intercourse has been shown to give more live births than clomiphene.” According to the data ESHRE summarises, what is correct?

options.text: Correct: two RCTs showed more live births with letrozole.
options.why: Neither cited RCT reports live birth; one found no difference in ongoing pregnancy.

options.text: A 270-woman RCT found more clinical pregnancies with letrozole, but the guideline reports no live birth data for this comparison and recommends no drug.
options.why: Correct: 23.07% versus 10.68% clinical pregnancy, with more multiple pregnancies with clomiphene; another RCT (172 women) found no difference in ongoing pregnancy.

options.text: It is the other way round: clomiphene gave more pregnancies and fewer multiple pregnancies.
options.why: In the 270-woman RCT, letrozole gave more clinical pregnancies and clomiphene more multiple pregnancies.

options.text: ESHRE recommends letrozole over clomiphene (conditional).
options.why: ESHRE makes no recommendation on which drug to use.

items.explanation: More clinical pregnancies in a small RCT do not equal more live births; moreover, stimulation alone is not supported in this indication.

items.stem: You are about to perform an oil-based contrast HSG in a woman with unexplained infertility. According to ESHRE, which precaution relates to its main risk?

options.text: Give antibiotic prophylaxis, because it increases infections.
options.why: ESHRE describes no difference in infection or haemorrhage between contrasts.

options.text: Always perform it under general anaesthesia.
options.why: This is not the precaution ESHRE proposes; it stresses fluoroscopic control.

options.text: None, because oil-based contrast is safer than water-based contrast.
options.why: Intravasation is more frequent with oil-based contrast (OR 5.00; 95% CI 2.25–11.12; in a study of 3,289 HSGs, 4.8% versus 1.3%).

options.text: Perform it under fluoroscopic control so that it can be stopped if intravasation occurs.
options.why: Correct: intravasation is more frequent with oil-based contrast (OR 5.00) and four cases of serious embolism have been reported since 1928.

items.explanation: Benefit (more clinical pregnancies and, in the largest trial's follow-up, more live births) versus risk (intravasation, rare embolism): hence shared decision-making and fluoroscopy.

items.stem: How does ESHRE frame its position on oil-based contrast HSG in unexplained infertility?

options.text: Mandatory for all couples (strong; ⊕⊕⊕⊕).
options.why: The recommendation is conditional with low certainty, not strong or high certainty.

options.text: Not recommended, because of the risk of embolism.
options.why: ESHRE considers it preferable; the risk is managed with counselling and fluoroscopic control.

options.text: Preferable to water-based contrast, discussing risks and benefits with all couples (conditional; ⊕⊕○○).
options.why: Correct: it is a conditional recommendation that requires shared decision-making.

options.text: Only for women with known tubal obstruction.
options.why: The recommendation addresses all couples with unexplained infertility.

items.explanation: In the meta-analysis cited, oil-based contrast probably increases clinical pregnancy (OR 1.42; 1.10–1.85), and in the 5-year follow-up of the largest trial there were more live births (RR 1.11; 1.03–1.20).

items.stem: How many stimulated IUI cycles do ESHRE and NICE envisage in unexplained infertility?

options.text: Both, a maximum of 2 cycles.
options.why: Neither sets that maximum: ESHRE speaks of 3–6 and NICE of up to 4.

options.text: ESHRE, up to 4; NICE, three to six.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.text: Both, unlimited cycles as long as the response is monofollicular.
options.why: Both guidelines envisage a limited number of cycles.

options.text: ESHRE, three to six cycles in its justification; NICE, up to 4 cycles with gonadotrophins before IVF.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE 3–6 (justification) and NICE “up to 4” (1.38.3).

items.explanation: Agree the number of cycles with the couple in advance: 3–6 in ESHRE's justification versus “up to 4” in the NICE recommendation.

items.stem: For IUI in a couple with unexplained infertility, a colleague proposes raising the gonadotrophin dose to obtain 4–5 follicles “to increase the chances”. What is appropriate?

options.text: Do it: more follicles increase live birth with no added risk.
options.why: The purpose of the low dose is precisely to avoid multiple pregnancy and OHSS.

options.text: Do it, as long as a single embryo is transferred.
options.why: There is no embryo transfer in IUI: the number of follicles determines the risk of multiple pregnancy.

options.text: Do not do it: ESHRE advises a low dose with monitoring (GPP) to avoid many follicles, and NICE the lowest effective dose.
options.why: Correct: according to ESHRE, a low dose greatly reduces multiple pregnancy without significantly reducing live birth; NICE 1.54.3 asks for the lowest effective dose and duration.

options.text: Do it, but only in the first cycle.
options.why: Neither guideline supports a high dose in any cycle in this indication.

items.explanation: Low dose with adequate monitoring (ESHRE GPP) and the lowest effective dose (NICE 1.54.3): this is how multiple pregnancy and OHSS are limited in stimulated IUI.

items.stem: Compared with expectant management, the OR for multiple pregnancy with stimulated IUI was 3.01 (95% CI 0.47–19.28; 2 RCTs). What is the correct reading?

options.text: It shows that stimulated IUI triples multiple pregnancy.
options.why: The point estimate is 3.01, but the interval includes 1: it is not significant.

options.text: A very imprecise, non-significant estimate: it neither shows nor rules out an increased risk.
options.why: Correct: the interval is very wide and includes 1; this is why ESHRE still insists on low dose and monitoring.

options.text: It shows that stimulated IUI does not increase multiple pregnancy.
options.why: A non-significant result with such a wide interval does not show absence of risk.

options.text: It shows that multiple pregnancy is lower than with expectant management.
options.why: An OR above 1 does not indicate a lower risk, and the interval includes 1.

items.explanation: Imprecision is not safety: with such a wide CI, prevention (low dose, monitoring) remains the rule.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with unexplained infertility and no previous treatment asks whether IVF would give her a higher chance of live birth than stimulated IUI. According to the data ESHRE summarises, what do you tell her?

options.text: In treatment-naïve women under 38 there was no difference (RR 1.01; 95% CI 0.88–1.15).
options.why: Correct: 3 RCTs, 925 women; hence ESHRE considers IVF probably not recommended over stimulated IUI (conditional).

options.text: Yes: IVF increases live birth by 54% in all women.
options.why: The overall RR of 1.54 does not hold in the treatment-naïve under-38 subgroup, which is hers.

options.text: Yes, and IVF also has less multiple pregnancy and OHSS.
options.why: The meta-analysis showed no significant difference in multiple pregnancy or OHSS.

options.text: No: stimulated IUI gives significantly more live births than IVF.
options.why: Not that either: in her subgroup there was no difference in either direction.

items.explanation: Apply the subgroup that matches the patient: treatment-naïve and <38 years, IVF and stimulated IUI do not differ in live birth.

items.stem: In the NHS (UK), a 40-year-old woman with unexplained fertility problems has not conceived after 2 years of regular unprotected intercourse and has never had IVF. According to NICE NG257, what is she offered?

options.text: 3 full cycles, with up to 3 more considered.
options.why: That applies to those under 40 (1.39.6, 1.39.7).

options.text: 1 full cycle of IVF.
options.why: Correct: at 40–41, if she meets the criteria in 1.39.3 and has not had IVF before, NICE offers 1 full cycle (1.39.9).

options.text: None, because ESHRE's definition limits unexplained infertility to ≤40 years.
options.why: NICE's 42nd-birthday limit is an NHS access criterion, independent of ESHRE's definition.

options.text: First, 4 mandatory IUI cycles.
options.why: NICE offers IVF after 2 years, with or without previous IUI; the 4 IUI cycles are something to consider, not a requirement.

items.explanation: NICE: IVF before the 42nd birthday after 2 years (1.39.3); 3 full cycles under 40 and 1 at 40–41 if there has been no previous IVF (1.39.9).

items.stem: According to NICE NG257, what does a “full cycle” of IVF comprise?

options.text: A single fresh embryo transfer.
options.why: A full cycle also includes transfer of the resulting frozen embryos.

options.text: Three consecutive ovarian stimulations.
options.why: A full cycle is a single episode of ovarian stimulation.

options.text: One stimulation and up to 2 transfers, whatever embryos remain.
options.why: NICE includes the transfer of all resulting embryos, not a fixed number.

options.text: One episode of ovarian stimulation and the transfer of all resulting fresh and frozen embryos.
options.why: Correct: this is NICE's definition (1.39.4).

items.explanation: When counting NHS-funded IVF cycles, NICE uses this definition of a full cycle (1.39.4).

items.stem: In which of these situations does NICE NG257 consider ICSI?

options.text: A previous IVF cycle with failed fertilisation or a very low fertilisation rate.
options.why: Correct: NICE considers ICSI with abnormal semen parameters (taking severity into account) or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2).

options.text: Unexplained infertility with a normal semen analysis, to secure fertilisation.
options.why: NICE advises not using ICSI for non-male factor fertility problems with normal semen parameters (1.50.3).

options.text: A 39-year-old woman with a normal semen analysis, because of her age.
options.why: Female age is not among the indications; with normal semen and a non-male factor, NICE advises against it.

options.text: Any couple paying for the procedure.
options.why: NICE's indications are clinical: abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation.

items.explanation: NICE draws a clear line: consider ICSI with abnormal semen or previous failed fertilisation (1.50.2); do not use it for non-male factor with normal semen (1.50.3).

items.stem: How do the two 2023 ESHRE documents (unexplained infertility guideline and add-ons document) rate ICSI without a male factor?

options.text: Guideline: conditional against; add-ons: “can be considered”.
options.why: The guideline is strong against and the add-ons document uses “not recommended”.

options.text: Guideline: strong against; add-ons: “currently not recommended for routine clinical use”.
options.why: In the add-ons document, ICSI for non-male factor is rated “not recommended”.

options.text: Guideline: not recommended over conventional IVF (strong; ⊕○○○); add-ons: “not recommended”.
options.why: Correct: both documents agree on not recommending it, each with its own scale.

options.text: Neither addresses it.
options.why: Both expressly address it, against.

items.explanation: In the RCTs reviewed, live birth was similar (35.5% with IVF versus 36.7% with ICSI; RR 1.03; 0.79–1.35), with greater resources and costs for ICSI.

items.stem: A woman with unexplained infertility asks about myo-inositol for herself and antioxidants for both partners “to help”. According to ESHRE, what is correct?

options.text: ESHRE recommends inositol (strong), but not antioxidants.
options.why: Inositol in women is considered probably not recommended (conditional; ⊕○○○).

options.text: ESHRE recommends antioxidants only for the man.
options.why: The conditional recommendation against covers both women and men.

options.text: ESHRE considers them probably not recommended (conditional; ⊕○○○); as good practice it does endorse a healthy diet, regular exercise and psychological support.
options.why: Correct: adjunct oral antioxidants in both partners and inositol in women, conditional against; lifestyle and psychological support, GPP.

options.text: ESHRE has a strong recommendation against both.
options.why: This overstates the strength: both are conditional recommendations.

items.explanation: From an integrative perspective, what ESHRE supports in this indication is lifestyle and psychological support, not antioxidants or inositol.

items.stem: In unexplained infertility, which of these interventions carries a STRONG recommendation against in ESHRE (not just a conditional one)?

options.text: Endometrial scratching.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE states that it should not be offered (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

options.text: Acupuncture in women.
options.why: It is a conditional recommendation (⊕⊕○○): probably not recommended.

options.text: Inositol in women.
options.why: It is a conditional recommendation (⊕○○○).

options.text: Adjunct oral antioxidants.
options.why: It is a conditional recommendation (⊕○○○), in women and men.

items.explanation: Different strength, same direction: scratching, strong against; acupuncture, inositol and antioxidants, conditional against.

items.stem: In the most recent RCT of endometrial scratching with timed intercourse (220 women) cited by ESHRE, live birth was 9% versus 7% with a sham procedure (OR 1.39; 95% CI 0.50–4.03). How should it be read?

options.text: It has been shown to increase live birth by 39%.
options.why: The OR of 1.39 has an interval that includes 1: it is not significant.

options.text: It reduces live birth compared with sham.
options.why: 9% versus 7% does not indicate a reduction, and the difference is not significant.

options.text: It is significant because 9% is higher than 7%.
options.why: Significance depends on the confidence interval, which here includes 1.

options.text: No significant difference: the interval includes 1.
options.why: Correct: overall, ESHRE concludes that the evidence does not show better pregnancy outcomes with scratching before intercourse or IUI.

items.explanation: A few small individual RCTs reported more pregnancies, but overall there is no benefit: hence scratching should not be offered (strong; ⊕⊕○○).

items.title: Case: Ana, Tomás and “test us for everything”

steps.text: Ana (fictional case), 34, no previous pregnancies, regular 27–31-day cycles, no history of PID and no endometriosis symptoms. Tomás, 36. They have been trying for 14 months.
